title: Why choosing family as executor of your will could put them in strife

 By Phoebe Loomes October 19 2026 - 4:00pm By Phoebe Loomes October 19 2026 - 4:00pm Save Share Choosing a family member or close friend to handle your affairs after your death might seem like a logical choice, but legal experts warn that being the executor of a will can quickly turn into a nightmare for your loved ones .

 Continue with Email Continue with Google Continue with Apple "I've come across so many clients who have seen it as a real burden that has been thrust upon them," Jeff Garrett, Legal Practice Director at Queensland law firm Attwood Marshall Lawyers, told The Senior. 
 "A lot of people simply appoint their family members or their children as executors, and I don't think anyone really knows how onerous the job is."
 Being an executor is a difficult role and can quickly turn into a paperwork nightmare for your loved ones, warns lawyer Jeff Garrett (right). Left file picture by ACM, right picture supplied While the burden can be heavy for family members, Garrett has also seen friends of the deceased struggle to manage difficult estates, and many end up feeling like the difficult role has been forced on them.
 "The worst people affected by this are not only family members, but close friends, who knew the deceased all their lives, then suddenly this responsibility is thrust upon them," he said.
 "Many don't even know until the person dies that they're the executor.
 "It's stressful. There are personal or potential personal liabilities that apply if you don't do the right thing, and it's a hairy role."
 What is involved in being an executor?
 Ever wondered what executors are responsible for when handling an estate?  Some of the things executors must do include:
 Secure probate - Probate is granted by the courts, and declares a will legally valid, giving the executor the ability to manage and distribute the estate. Where a will is straightforward, this process usually takes between two and eight weeks.
 Close accounts of the deceased -  Executors are responsible for closing accounts used by the deceased including bank accounts, and phone and internet accounts. But Garrett said many companies will not allow executors to act until after probate is granted, and may even require a copy of the death certificate..
 File remaining tax returns - Deceased estates often require the executor to complete a final tax return, and settle any outstanding debts with the Australian Taxation Office.
 Settle debts - The executor will take on responsibility for handling outstanding debts. Where this is mishandled, executors can become personally liable.
 Distributing assets - The executor is responsible for distributing funds, assets and personal items to all beneficiaries.
 Executors must meet complex legal requirements
 Even what are considered simpler estates often may include property, cars, a caravan, superannuation and sometimes investment properties.
 They also need to finalise tax returns, wind up any business interests, and close phone and bank accounts.
 Many struggle with the paperwork, and most companies will require a death certificate and completion of probate before allowing accounts to be closed.
 "It all adds up," said Garrett, who has spent more than four decades handling wills and estates.
 Garrett also warned that executors face legal requirements, and can get themselves into serious trouble if they mishandle an estate, even by mistake.
 "The ATO is just so militant with how they approach these things," he said.
 "If you do the wrong thing, you could be held personally liable as executor of the estate for any tax debts."
 The role of executor particularly tricky in blended families
 Garrett said in blended families, where both partners may have children from previous marriages, it can often help to work with an independent voice.
 "Quite often the two parties want to provide for their children from their previous marriage," he said.
 "In a blended family, it usually causes problems because whoever the surviving spouse is can change their will and leave everything to their own children, and not provide for their deceased spouse's children."
 Families wanting to avoid this should consider appointing a co-executor to serve alongside the spouse, and consider setting up a trust to benefit all the children after the death of both parents, he said.
 "In a lot of cases you need to appoint a co-executor with the spouse," he said.
 "Usually a lawyer is a good idea [as co-executor], because if you appoint one of the adult children, that can also cause problems, disharmony and arguments."
 Want to appoint an independent person as executor? Here's what to do
 Garrett recommended spending time researching legal firms, including checking testimonials on their website, and looking at reviews.
 "You've just got to do your own research and find people who have a good reputation in the community, and generally among lawyers or their peers," he said.
 He warned that choosing a more general lawyer to handle your estate could also be a mistake, and recommended finding someone with a specialty in estates.
 "There are people out there, conveyancers and things ... who honestly they don't have a clue what they're doing," he said.
 "They're not much better than the man on the street."
